Theodore von Kármán. Hungarian-American aerodynamicist and physicist who pioneered the theory of transonic and supersonic flow, turbulence, and rocket propulsion. Though primarily a theorist, Kármán was the intellectual godfather of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and shaped American military and civilian rocket programs through mentorship and scientific authority.

He founded and directed the Jet Propulsion Laboratory at Caltech — the premier American rocket research facility, which became NASA's center for planetary exploration. Kármán developed rigorous mathematical theories of aerodynamic drag, shock waves, and hypersonic flow, providing the theoretical underpinning for rocket and missile design. He mentored and collaborated with Wernher von Braun, Frank Malina, and a generation of American rocket engineers, lending scientific credibility to spaceflight when it was derided as fantasy.

Kármán advised the U.S. military on ballistic missile and rocket propulsion programs. His authority gave rocketry legitimacy in American defense circles. He published seminal papers on turbulence theory and nonlinear fluid dynamics that remain foundational to aerospace engineering.

He lived through two World Wars and emigrated from Europe to America, becoming a symbol of European scientific genius enriching American innovation.
